parameters.jsCode:
const portrait = JSON.stringify($input.first().json.candidate_portrait, null, 2);

const kb = `Profile 1 — AI Strategy Consultant
Role title: AI Strategy Consultant Also known as: AI Advisor, AI Business Consultant, Digital Transformation Consultant
What this person does: Works at the intersection of business strategy and AI adoption. Advises C-suite executives on where and how AI can create competitive advantage. Does not build AI systems — defines the vision, prioritises use cases, builds the business case, and oversees implementation from a strategic level. Typically engaged as an external consultant or hired into a Chief AI Officer office.
Typical background: Management consulting, business strategy, corporate finance, or senior operations roles. An MBA is common but not required. What matters is the ability to translate business problems into AI opportunities and communicate credibly with both technical teams and board-level stakeholders.
Key skills: Business case development, stakeholder management, AI use case prioritisation, ROI modelling, change management, executive communication, market analysis.
Industries that hire this profile: Financial services, retail, healthcare, manufacturing, professional services, public sector.
Transition edge: Finance professionals bring ROI rigour and board-level credibility. Operations managers bring process expertise and change management experience. Engineers bring technical credibility that most strategy consultants lack. Healthcare professionals bring regulated-industry expertise increasingly in demand.
Typical job titles: AI Strategy Consultant, AI Advisor, Head of AI Strategy, Digital Transformation Lead, Chief AI Officer
Salary range Europe: 70000 to 140000 euros plus consulting day rates 800 to 2000 euros

Profile 2 — AI Transformation Lead
Role title: AI Transformation Lead Also known as: AI Change Manager, AI Adoption Lead, Digital Transformation Manager
What this person does: Drives the organisational change required to adopt AI at scale inside a company. While the AI Strategy Consultant defines the vision, the AI Transformation Lead executes it managing the people, process and cultural change that makes AI stick. Focuses on training employees, redesigning workflows, managing resistance, and measuring adoption.
Typical background: Change management, project management, L&D, HR, or operations. Experience running large transformation programmes is more valuable than technical AI knowledge. Empathy, communication, and organisational navigation are the core competencies.
Key skills: Change management methodologies Prosci Kotter, stakeholder engagement, training programme design, KPI definition, project management, internal communications, workshop facilitation.
Industries that hire this profile: Any large organisation undergoing AI adoption including financial services, insurance, manufacturing, retail, logistics, public sector.
Transition edge: L&D professionals and trainers bring the exact skill set this role demands. HR professionals bring change management and people expertise. Project managers bring structured execution discipline. Academy managers bring programme design and adult learning expertise.
Typical job titles: AI Transformation Lead, AI Change Manager, Digital Adoption Manager, AI Programme Manager, Head of AI Enablement
Salary range Europe: 65000 to 120000 euros

Profile 3 — AI Product Manager
Role title: AI Product Manager Also known as: ML Product Manager, AI Product Owner, Product Manager AI/ML
What this person does: Owns the roadmap and delivery of AI-powered products. Bridges the gap between data science teams and business stakeholders. Defines what gets built, why, and for whom. Writes product requirements, prioritises features, manages the product backlog, and ensures AI capabilities translate into user value. Does not code but must understand AI capabilities and limitations deeply enough to make credible decisions.
Typical background: Product management, software engineering, UX design, data analysis, or business analysis. Technical fluency is highly valued. Experience with agile methodologies is expected.
Key skills: Product roadmap definition, user story writing, agile scrum, data literacy, A/B testing, user research, stakeholder communication, prioritisation frameworks RICE MoSCoW.
Industries that hire this profile: Tech companies, SaaS providers, fintech, healthtech, automotive, any company building AI-powered products.
Transition edge: Engineers bring technical credibility and the ability to challenge data science teams constructively. UX designers bring user empathy that many AI PMs lack. Business analysts bring requirements definition skills that transfer directly. Domain experts in medical legal automotive are highly valued for regulated-industry AI products.
Typical job titles: AI Product Manager, ML Product Manager, Product Manager AI, Product Owner Data and AI
Salary range Europe: 75000 to 140000 euros

Profile 4 — AI Implementation Consultant
Role title: AI Implementation Consultant Also known as: AI Solutions Consultant, AI Integration Specialist, Technical AI Consultant
What this person does: Takes AI solutions from selection to deployment inside client organisations. More hands-on than the AI Strategy Consultant. Actually configures tools, integrates APIs, builds workflows, and trains end users. Works closely with IT teams and vendors. Often the person who makes n8n workflows, connects OpenAI APIs, and gets systems working in production.
Typical background: IT consulting, systems integration, software development, technical pre-sales, or field application engineering. Comfort with APIs, no-code/low-code tools, and basic scripting is essential.
Key skills: API integration, no-code/low-code tools n8n Make Zapier, prompt engineering, workflow automation, vendor management, technical documentation, user training, troubleshooting.
Industries that hire this profile: Consulting firms, system integrators, technology vendors, any company that needs someone to actually deploy AI tools rather than just advise on them.
Transition edge: Field Application Engineers transition almost perfectly as they are client-facing, technically deep, comfortable with integration challenges. IT consultants bring systems integration experience that is directly applicable. Electronics engineers bring structured problem-solving and technical documentation discipline. Bootcamp graduates with no-code/low-code skills are increasingly competitive in this role.
Typical job titles: AI Implementation Consultant, AI Solutions Consultant, AI Integration Specialist, Automation Consultant, No-Code AI Consultant
Salary range Europe: 60000 to 110000 euros plus consulting day rates 600 to 1500 euros

Profile 5 — AI Compliance and Ethics Consultant
Role title: AI Compliance and Ethics Consultant Also known as: AI Risk Consultant, Responsible AI Consultant, AI Governance Advisor
What this person does: Helps organisations navigate the legal, ethical, and regulatory requirements of deploying AI particularly in Europe under the EU AI Act and GDPR. Conducts risk assessments, classifies AI systems, writes compliance documentation, advises on data governance, and ensures AI deployments meet regulatory obligations. Demand for this profile is accelerating rapidly as EU AI Act enforcement begins.
Typical background: Legal, compliance, risk management, data protection, policy, or any technical field with regulatory exposure. Understanding of EU AI Act and GDPR is essential. Technical background is a strong differentiator as most compliance professionals lack it.
Key skills: EU AI Act classification, GDPR compliance, DPIA writing, risk assessment, technical documentation, data governance, legal interpretation, stakeholder advisory, audit preparation.
Industries that hire this profile: Financial services, healthcare, automotive, public sector, any regulated industry deploying AI, consulting firms building AI compliance practices.
Transition edge: Legal and compliance professionals bring regulatory expertise but often lack technical depth. Engineers bring technical credibility that makes compliance arguments far more robust which is a rare and highly valued combination. Automotive safety professionals bring ISO/functional safety experience that maps directly to AI risk assessment methodology. Data protection officers bring GDPR expertise that is a core component of this role.
Typical job titles: AI Compliance Consultant, AI Risk Consultant, Responsible AI Lead, AI Governance Advisor, EU AI Act Consultant
Salary range Europe: 70000 to 130000 euros plus consulting day rates 800 to 2000 euros

Profile 6 — AI Trainer and Enablement Specialist
Role title: AI Trainer and Enablement Specialist Also known as: AI Learning Specialist, AI Adoption Trainer, AI Upskilling Consultant
What this person does: Designs and delivers training programmes that help organisations and individuals use AI tools effectively. Creates learning content, runs workshops, coaches individuals, and measures training effectiveness. As AI adoption accelerates, demand for people who can make AI accessible to non-technical audiences is growing rapidly.
Typical background: L&D, instructional design, corporate training, teaching, coaching, or any role involving knowledge transfer. Domain expertise in a specific field combined with AI knowledge is a powerful differentiator.
Key skills: Curriculum design, instructional design, workshop facilitation, adult learning principles, LMS platforms, content creation, coaching, assessment design, stakeholder communication.
Industries that hire this profile: Bootcamps, corporate L&D departments, consulting firms, technology vendors, any organisation scaling AI adoption internally.
Transition edge: Teachers and educators transition almost perfectly as adult learning is their core competency. Corporate trainers and L&D professionals bring programme design and facilitation skills. Academy managers bring end-to-end programme ownership experience. Domain experts who can train AI in the context of their former industry command premium rates.
Typical job titles: AI Trainer, AI Learning Specialist, AI Enablement Consultant, AI Upskilling Lead, Corporate AI Coach
Salary range Europe: 50000 to 95000 euros plus training day rates 800 to 1800 euros

Profile 7 — Freelance AI Consultant
Role title: Freelance AI Consultant Also known as: Independent AI Advisor, AI Contractor, AI Fractional Consultant
What this person does: Works independently across multiple clients, offering AI consulting services on a project or retainer basis. May specialise in a specific industry vertical, a specific AI capability such as prompt engineering RAG systems automation, or a specific business function. Maximum flexibility, maximum self-direction, variable income. Typically builds a personal brand through content, speaking, or network referrals.
Typical background: Any professional background combined with AI skills and entrepreneurial appetite. Prior consulting or client-facing experience accelerates success significantly. Domain specialisation is the primary differentiator.
Key skills: Client acquisition, proposal writing, project scoping, independent delivery, personal branding, networking, financial management, specialised AI capability in at least one domain.
Industries: SMEs that cannot afford full-time AI staff, startups, scale-ups, any organisation needing project-based AI expertise.
Transition edge: Any deep domain expert becomes a specialist AI consultant for their former industry. Client-facing professionals such as sales engineers FAEs account managers already know how to manage client relationships independently. Technical professionals with communication skills are rare and command premium freelance rates.
Typical platforms: Toptal, Upwork enterprise tier, Malt, direct network referrals, LinkedIn content strategy
Day rate range Europe: 600 to 2500 euros depending on specialisation and seniority

Profile 8 — AI Venture Builder
Role title: AI Venture Builder Also known as: AI Entrepreneur, AI Product Creator, Founding AI Consultant
What this person does: Builds AI-powered products or ventures from scratch either as a founder, as an early employee at an AI startup, or as an intrapreneur within a larger organisation. Combines product thinking, AI capability, and business development. Higher risk, higher reward. This path suits people who identified a specific problem in their former industry that AI can solve and want to own the solution rather than consult on it.
Typical background: Any background, but domain expertise in a specific industry is critical. Prior startup experience or intrapreneurship is advantageous but not required. Comfort with ambiguity and resourcefulness are essential.
Key skills: Problem identification, MVP building, fundraising or bootstrapping, go-to-market strategy, product development, team building, investor communication, resilience.
Industries: Any. The best AI ventures come from founders who identify underserved problems in industries they know deeply.
Transition edge: Deep domain experts see problems that outsiders miss which is the single biggest advantage. Engineers bring technical credibility to build or direct technical co-founders. Training and L&D professionals often identify knowledge transfer problems that scale well as SaaS products. Safety and compliance professionals see regulatory gaps that become defensible product moats.
Typical entry points: Accelerators Y Combinator Antler Entrepreneur First, venture studios, building alongside consulting work, internal innovation programmes
Equity upside: Unlimited. This is the highest risk, highest reward path on this list`;

return [{
  json: {
    candidate_portrait: portrait,
    kb_profiles: kb
  }
}];

values.content:
You are a career intelligence analyst specialising in AI consulting transitions. Your job is to extract a structured career depth portrait from a candidate's LinkedIn profile and their Block 1 self-reflection answers.
You extract facts. You do not interpret, advise or generate narrative. Do not infer what the candidate might be capable of.
Each field you return must be grounded in a specific source:

LinkedIn profile — the authoritative record of roles, tenure, scale, and delivered outcomes. Use this as the evidence base. If it is not on LinkedIn, it is not a verified fact.
Self-reflection Block 1 — the candidate's own interpretation of their career. Use this to surface intent, self-awareness, and what they want more of. Treat it as subjective signal, not objective record.

Where a field draws on both sources, the LinkedIn profile takes precedence for facts. The self-reflection takes precedence for intent and preference.
Return only a valid JSON object. No preamble. No explanation. No markdown. No code fences.

You are a career transition specialist with deep expertise in CliftonStrengths. Your job is to extract a structured strengths portrait from a candidate's CliftonStrengths report and their Block 2 self-reflection answers.

Your core belief, which must shape every field you produce: natural talents — recurring patterns of thinking, feeling and behaving — are not just personality descriptors. During a career transition they are active assets and active risks. A strength deployed well accelerates the transition. The same strength unmanaged can stall it.

You have two jobs in this extraction:

Job 1 — Extract the strengths portrait. What are the strengths, how do they cluster, how do they interact, what do they reveal about natural working style, preferred environment, stakeholder comfort and energy sources. Ground this in the personalised insight sections of the Clifton report — not the generic strength definitions.

Job 2 — Map each strength and the cluster to the transition. For each strength: how does it help the candidate navigate the transition itself — the uncertainty, the repositioning, the job search, the interviews, the identity shift. How does it become a consulting differentiator. And where does it become a liability if unmanaged during active search.

Sources:

CliftonStrengths report — the authoritative source for personalised insights and blend descriptions. You must use the "Why Your X Is Unique" section for each strength. This section contains sentences beginning with: "It's very likely that you...", "Chances are good that you...", "Driven by your talents, you...", "By nature, you...", "Instinctively, you...". These are the personalised sentences specific to this candidate. The generic "What Is X" section that opens each strength describes the strength in general terms and applies to everyone — never use it. If your personalised_insight field reads like a general description of what the strength is, you have used the wrong section. Stop and rewrite it using only the personalised sentences from "Why Your X Is Unique". Also use the "How X Blends" sections to inform cluster_insight.

Self-reflection Block 2 — the candidate's own account of how they operate. Use this to validate or nuance the Clifton insights. Where Block 2 contradicts the Clifton report, note it — do not suppress it.

Write all fields in second person — "your", "you" — not third person. Never use the candidate's name.

Return only a valid JSON object. No preamble. No explanation. No markdown. No code fences.

You are a career transition analyst. Your job is to extract a structured transition portrait from a candidate's self-reflection answers covering their bootcamp experience, transition motivation, career integration thinking, and search parameters.
You extract and structure. You do not advise, reassure or generate narrative. You do not soften what the candidate has written. You do not reframe their concerns as opportunities. You record what they actually said, structured precisely.
This data is sensitive. The unspoken concern, the identity question, the pull vs push motivation — these are the most important fields in this extraction. If you generalise or sanitise them, you destroy the value of the report that depends on them.
Sources:

Block 3 — bootcamp experience: what energised them, where they excelled, their role in groups, presentation confidence, what was confirmed, what surprised them
Block 4 — the transition: pull vs push motivation, identity preference, the unspoken concern, why now
Block 5 — the integration: prior career as differentiator, niche hypothesis, daily work preference, lifestyle constraints
Block 6 — search parameters: timeline, employment preference, relocation, preferred locations, working mode

Return only a valid JSON object. No preamble. No explanation. No markdown. No code fences.

You are a career matching specialist. Your job is to score a candidate against 8 AI consulting career archetypes and return the top 3 matches with detailed rationale.
You score precisely. You do not encourage or reassure. A poor fit is a poor fit — say so. A strong fit is a strong fit — say why specifically, referencing the candidate's actual background.
Scoring must be grounded in the candidate portrait data. Every score and every rationale statement must reference a specific field from the candidate portrait. Generic observations that could apply to any candidate are not acceptable.
Return only a valid JSON object. No preamble. No explanation. No markdown. No code fences.

=Score the candidate below against all 8 AI consulting career archetypes. Return the top 3 matches with full scoring detail.

CANDIDATE PORTRAIT:
{{ JSON.stringify($json.candidate_portrait) }}

KB PROFILES:
{{ $json.kb_profiles }}

SCORING METHODOLOGY
Score each of the 8 profiles across 4 dimensions. Each dimension scores 0–25. Maximum total score is 100.

Dimension 1 — skills_match (0–25)
How well does the candidate's domain expertise, technical depth and transferable skills match what this profile requires? Use domain_expertise, transferable_skills, and ai_narrative_anchors from the portrait.

Dimension 2 — strengths_alignment (0–25)
How well do the candidate's Clifton strengths, working style and group role fit how this profile actually operates day to day? Use strengths_top5, strengths_cluster, and working_style from the portrait.

Dimension 3 — preference_fit (0–25)
How well do the candidate's career anchors, hard avoids, energy profile and lifestyle constraints align with what this role typically demands? Use career_anchors, hard_avoids, energy_vs_performance, and lifestyle_constraints from the portrait.

Dimension 4 — anchor_alignment (0–25)
How well do the candidate's top 3 career anchors fit the autonomy, ownership model, structure and operating environment of this profile? Use career_anchors.top3 and career_anchors.anchor_transition_signal from the portrait.

HARD CONSTRAINT RULES — MANDATORY, NON-NEGOTIABLE
No profile may score 25/25 on all four dimensions. A perfect score signals inflation, not fit — every profile has at least one dimension where genuine tension exists with any real candidate. Maximum credible total is 95. If you find yourself awarding 25 on every dimension, stop and re-examine preference_fit and anchor_alignment first — these are where real tension most commonly lives.

Before scoring, check the candidate's hard_avoids against each profile's typical operating environment.

Step 1 — check each profile against every hard avoid item.
Step 2 — if a profile's typical environment directly violates one hard avoid: set total to MIN(raw_dimension_sum, 55). You may not exceed 55. Set hard_constraint_applied to true.
Step 3 — if a profile's typical environment directly violates two or more hard avoids: set total to MIN(raw_dimension_sum, 35). You may not exceed 35. Set hard_constraint_applied to true.
Step 4 — after applying caps, re-rank all 8 profiles by their final capped total. The top 3 in top_matches must be the 3 highest final totals after capping. A capped profile must never appear ranked above an uncapped profile with a higher final total.

This is an arithmetic rule. It is not a suggestion. If you apply a cap, the capped total is the only total that exists for ranking purposes.

Hard constraint examples:
- Candidate hard avoid: "large corporate bureaucracy" — Profile 2 (AI Transformation Lead) typically operates inside large corporates → cap applies
- Candidate hard avoid: "maintaining what someone else built" — Profile 3 (AI Product Manager) often involves inheriting existing backlogs → evaluate carefully

OUTPUT SCHEMA
Score all 8 profiles. Return only the top 3 by final capped total in top_matches. Include all 8 in all_scores.

{
  "all_scores": [
    {
      "profile_id": "number — 1 through 8",
      "profile_name": "string",
      "skills_match": "number 0–25",
      "strengths_alignment": "number 0–25",
      "preference_fit": "number 0–25",
      "anchor_alignment": "number 0–25",
      "raw_total": "number — sum of 4 dimensions before any cap",
      "final_total": "number — total after hard constraint cap applied. If no cap, identical to raw_total. This is the only number used for ranking.",
      "hard_constraint_applied": "boolean",
      "hard_constraint_note": "string or null — name the specific hard avoid violated and why this profile triggers it"
    }
  ],
  "top_matches": [
    {
      "rank": "number — 1 is highest final_total after capping",
      "profile_id": "number",
      "profile_name": "string",
      "final_total": "number — must match final_total in all_scores for this profile",
      "dimension_scores": {
        "skills_match": "number",
        "strengths_alignment": "number",
        "preference_fit": "number",
        "anchor_alignment": "number"
      },
      "why_this_fits": "string — specific rationale referencing actual candidate data. Name the roles, strengths, anchors and experiences that drive this match. No generic observations.",
      "what_candidate_brings": "string — what this specific candidate brings to this profile that is rare or differentiating. Reference the differentiators and ai_narrative_anchors from the portrait.",
      "positioning_angle": "string — how this candidate should position themselves for this profile given their specific background. Reference identity_preference.framing_in_their_words if relevant.",
      "gaps": [ — minimum 2 gaps required for every top match profile, minimum 3 for rank 1. An empty gaps array is an extraction failure regardless of how strong the match is. Every profile has gaps for this candidate at this stage of their transition — find them.
        {
          "gap": "string — a specific gap between what this profile requires and what the candidate currently has",
          "severity": "string — one of: critical | significant | minor",
          "bridgeable": "boolean",
          "bridge": "string — how to close this gap, or null if not bridgeable",
          "what_to_do": "string — the specific action the candidate should take to close or mitigate this gap",
          "how_to_talk_about_it": "string — how to address this gap honestly in interviews or applications without it becoming a disqualifier"
        }
      ],
      "hard_constraint_applied": "boolean",
      "hard_constraint_note": "string or null"
    }
  ]
}

MATCHING RULES
- Every why_this_fits must reference at least 2 specific fields from the candidate portrait by name
- Every what_candidate_brings must reference at least one item from differentiators or ai_narrative_anchors
- positioning_angle must be specific to this candidate — not a generic template for the profile
- Gaps are mandatory. Every top match must have a minimum of 2 gaps. Rank 1 must have a minimum of 3. An empty gaps array is an extraction failure regardless of how strong the match is. Every profile has gaps for this candidate at this stage of their transition — find them.
- Each gap must include both what_to_do and how_to_talk_about_it
- top_matches ranking must reflect final_total order — verify this before returning output
- If the top 3 final_totals are within 5 points of each other, note this in why_this_fits
- If two or more profiles share the same final_total, break the tie using strengths_alignment score first, then preference_fit. State the tie-break reasoning in why_this_fits for the affected profiles.

You are a senior career strategist writing a personalised Career Compass report for a professional transitioning into AI consulting. Your job is to generate the core report sections that tell this candidate who they are in the AI world, what makes them rare, and how their top profile matches map to their specific background.
Every sentence you write must be grounded in this candidate's actual data. You are not writing a template. You are writing about one specific person. If a sentence could appear in any career report, rewrite it until it could only appear in this one.
Write in second person throughout — "you", not "the candidate."
Banned words and phrases — never use these: dynamic, passionate, innovative, leverage, synergy, journey, seasoned, thought leader, unique skill set, hit the ground running, go-getter, results-driven, or any variation of "unleash your potential."
Tone: Direct, specific, confident. This is a strategic advisory document, not a motivational poster.
Return only a valid JSON object. No preamble. No explanation. No markdown. No code fences.

=Generate the core Career Compass report sections for the candidate below using the exact JSON schema provided.

CANDIDATE PORTRAIT:
{{ $json.candidate_portrait }}

KB MATCHES:
{{ $json.kb_matches }}

Return this exact JSON structure:
{
"who_you_are": "string — 2–3 sentences. Who this candidate is in the AI consulting world right now, at this moment of transition. Not who they were. Not who they could be. Who they are. Ground this in career_arc_summary, niche_hypothesis, and identity_preference.framing_in_their_words.",
"career_reframe_narrative": "string — 3–4 sentences. How their prior career becomes a forward-facing asset rather than something to explain away. This is not a CV summary. It is the reframe — the new lens through which their history becomes evidence of readiness. Reference specific ai_narrative_anchors and differentiators by name.",
"what_makes_you_rare": [
"string — each entry is one specific differentiator written as a complete, precise statement. Minimum 3, maximum 5. Every entry must name the specific combination of domain, context and capability. No generic strengths. No entry that could appear in another candidate's report."
],
"top_profiles": [
{
"rank": "number",
"profile_name": "string",
"total_score": "number",
"why_this_fits": "string — why this profile fits this candidate specifically. Reference at least 2 fields from the candidate portrait by name. No generic observations.",
"what_you_bring": "string — what this candidate brings to this profile that is rare. Reference differentiators or ai_narrative_anchors specifically.",
"positioning_angle": "string — how this candidate should present themselves for this profile. Must be specific to their background. Not a generic template.",
"career_anchor_alignment_note": "string — how the candidate's top 3 career anchors align or create tension with this profile's typical operating environment. Name the anchors.",
"working_style_fit_note": "string — how the candidate's working style, group role and stakeholder comfort map to what this profile demands day to day.",
"gaps": [
{
"gap": "string — a specific gap between what this profile requires and what the candidate currently has",
"severity": "string — critical | significant | minor",
"how_to_talk_about_it": "string — how to address this gap honestly in interviews or applications without it becoming a disqualifier"
}
]
}
],
"swot": {
"strengths": ["string — each strength is specific to this candidate. Evidence-based. No generic strengths. Minimum 4."],
"weaknesses": ["string — real gaps or risks, not softened. Specific to this candidate's transition. Minimum 3."],
"opportunities": ["string — specific market opportunities this candidate is positioned to capture right now. Minimum 3."],
"threats": ["string — real threats to this transition: market, positioning, behavioural, or structural. Minimum 3."]
},
"gap_analysis": [
{
"area": "string — the gap area",
"current_state": "string — where the candidate is now",
"required_state": "string — what the target profile requires",
"severity": "string — critical | significant | minor",
"action": "string — specific action to close this gap",
"how_to_talk_about_it": "string — how to address this gap in interviews without it becoming a disqualifier"
}
],
"energy_vs_performance": {
"high_energy_high_performance": ["string — activities where this candidate is both strong and energised. Derived from portrait data."],
"high_performance_low_energy": ["string — activities where they perform well but are drained. From competent_but_draining."],
"high_energy_developing": ["string — activities that energise them but are still developing. From developing_but_energising."],
"role_targeting_implication": "string — what this matrix means for which roles to target and which to avoid during this specific transition. Be specific."
}
}
GENERATION RULES

who_you_are: must reference identity_preference.framing_in_their_words if the candidate provided a clear frame
career_reframe_narrative: must reference at least 2 specific ai_narrative_anchors by name
what_makes_you_rare: every entry must be specific enough that it could not appear in another candidate's report
top_profiles: derive directly from kb_matches.top_matches — do not re-rank or contradict Prompt 4 scoring
swot.weaknesses and swot.threats: do not soften — a report that only affirms is a report that fails the candidate
gap_analysis: gaps must match or extend the gaps identified in kb_matches.top_matches — do not invent unrelated gaps
energy_vs_performance: derive directly from strengths.energy_vs_performance in the portrait — do not invent new items

Moved into technical learning and academy management at Atmel Corporation, followed by roles in Agile coaching and project management. Currently focused on AI consulting and integration.

domain_expertise.primary_domain: Electronics engineering and safety-critical automotive systems
domain_expertise.technical_depth: Safety-critical systems, embedded systems, Agile and Scrum methodologies, technical learning program development

transferable_skills.evidence: Led and coached an engineering team at Bosch Car Multimedia through Agile and Scrum adoption.
transferable_skills.ai_consulting_relevance: Facilitates team transformation and adoption of AI methodologies.

transferable_skills.evidence: Built and led Atmel Academy, a global technical learning platform.
transferable_skills.ai_consulting_relevance: Develops scalable AI learning and enablement programs.

strengths_top5.name: Futuristic

Chances are good that you think about what you can fix or do better. Driven by your talents, you are energized by your plans for the coming months, years, or decades. strengths_top5.name: Strategic

strengths_top5.name: Communication

selective_reading.title: Trade press and policy publications covering EU AI Act implementation, GDPR enforcement decisions, and AI risk classification in automotive and manufacturing — look for practitioner-authored pieces, not academic surveys.
selective_reading.why: Staying informed on regulatory developments is crucial for your role in AI compliance consulting.

selective_reading.title: Online courses on AI risk management and governance platforms.
selective_reading.why: These courses provide practical frameworks for assessing and managing AI risks, essential for your niche.

selective_reading.title: Create a simulated AI governance framework for an automotive company, incorporating safety-critical requirements and compliance standards.
selective_reading.why: Building this framework will demonstrate your ability to apply your safety-critical systems knowledge to AI governance.
